title: absorb() reports FetchingDisabled when a fetch succeeded but added nothing
description:
pkix-chain/src/sans_io.rs:300-309. When absorb() finds that no certificate was added from a fetch round, it returns:

    Some(Error::Aia(state.last_aia_error.clone().unwrap_or(AiaError::FetchingDisabled)))

The unwrap_or is wrong when the fetch SUCCEEDED. A fetcher that returns a certificate already in the pool (a stale CA generation still published at its AIA URI, say, or a repository serving the same intermediate the caller supplied) produces no last_aia_error, so the caller is told AIA fetching is disabled. It was not: a request was made and answered.

Found while writing a test for PKIX-rm8.45, where this was one of two reports that outranked the one under test. The scenario is ordinary, not adversarial.

Suggested shape: a distinct AiaError for 'fetched, but nothing usable was added' -- the enum is #[non_exhaustive], so adding a variant is additive. FetchingDisabled should be reserved for the case where no fetch was attempted, which is what NoAiaFetcher means by it.

Note the existing precedence logic is sound and should be kept: a fetch attempted and failed outranks a URI never tried. This is only about the fallback value when nothing failed.
close_reason:
Fixed. AiaError::NoNewIssuer replaces the FetchingDisabled fallback.

The bead was mine, filed while writing the PKIX-rm8.45 test where this was one of two reports that outranked the one under test. Confirmed on re-reading the code: absorb() returns Error::Aia(state.last_aia_error.clone().unwrap_or(FetchingDisabled)) when a round adds nothing, and the fallback is reached EXACTLY when nothing failed -- so it claimed fetching was disabled in the one case where fetching had demonstrably worked.

Worse than inaccurate, it misdirects. An operator reads FetchingDisabled as "my fetcher is switched off" and audits configuration, while the fetcher is working and the repository is stale or mispointed.

Audited the paths that reach it before naming the variant. Three ways a successful round adds nothing: (1) the response held no CA certificate so nothing in it could be an issuer -- typically an AIA URI pointing at a leaf; (2) every certificate was already pooled -- a repository still publishing a stale CA generation; (3) it parsed to no certificates at all. Went with ONE variant, NoNewIssuer, since all three mean "AIA cannot help from here" and the operational difference is for debugging the repository rather than for control flow. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so splitting it later is additive if the distinction is ever wanted.

FetchingDisabled keeps its proper meaning: no request was made, which is what NoAiaFetcher means by it.

Precedence left alone, as the bead itself said to: a fetch attempted and failed still outranks this because it says more. Only the fallback changed.

Test: a_fetch_that_adds_nothing_is_not_reported_as_fetching_disabled in pkix-chain/tests/review_aia.rs. The fixture is an ordinary misconfiguration, not an attack -- the repository serves the same wrong-key intermediate the caller supplied. It asserts the fetch actually happened (f.count() == 1) so a passing test cannot mean "nothing was tried", and asserts both that the error IS NoNewIssuer and is NOT FetchingDisabled.

Verified by mutation: restoring the old fallback fails with "expected Aia(NoNewIssuer); got Aia(FetchingDisabled)".

Versions: pkix-aia 0.2.0 -> 0.2.1 (additive variant), pkix-chain 0.7.0 -> 0.7.1 (behaviour). Both are published, so both need a number to ship.

Gates green: fmt, clippy, rustdoc, typos, 2365 tests, workspace feature powerset clean.
